Robert Pollard.description: Robert Pollard's first billed solo album is basically an alternate-universe Guided by Voices record, cut mostly alone on a four-track with the same jump-cut editing and classic-rock-radio hooks buried in hiss, as on 'Party Times Sadness Eyes' and 'Get Under It.' Without a full band to push back, the songs feel even more like fragments of a much longer private tape than GBV albums of the same period. It confirmed that the home-taping method was Pollard's own voice, not just a byproduct of a particular lineup.
Robert Pollard.lineage: A parallel outlet to Guided by Voices' mid-1990s work, using the same Dayton four-track method and later feeding into Pollard's long-running Fading Captain solo series.

Rodney Crowell.description: Crowell's debut is a Nashville session all-star record wearing a rock and roll attitude: Emmylou Harris, Willie Nelson, Ricky Skaggs and Nicolette Larson sing background vocals while Ry Cooder and James Burton trade slide and dobro on a mix of covers (Eric Von Schmidt, Don Everly) and Crowell originals like the title track and Voila, an American Dream. It didn't chart, but the songs became a quiet standard-bearer catalog, later covered by everyone from the Oak Ridge Boys to Alan Jackson. Its loose, Telecaster-driven sound and refusal to chase a single set the pattern Crowell would keep returning to for the next decade.
Rodney Crowell.lineage: Grew directly out of Crowell's time in Emmylou Harris's Hot Band, and its loose, guest-heavy Nashville-outsider sound anticipates both the cowpunk/LA roots scene (V14) and Crowell's own late-'80s hits.

Rodney Crowell.description: After a decade of critically loved but commercially ignored records, Diamonds & Dirt became Crowell's breakthrough, setting a record with five consecutive number-one country singles including She's Crazy for Leavin' (co-written with Guy Clark) and a duet with Rosanne Cash on It's Such a Small World. Co-produced with Tony Brown, it keeps the same plainspoken, Telecaster-forward sound as Crowell's earlier records but with sharper hooks and tighter arrangements built for country radio. It proved the neotraditional, gloss-averse sound this whole lane is built around could still be a commercial country smash.
Rodney Crowell.lineage: The commercial vindication of the sound Crowell had been developing since Ain't Living Long Like This, co-written in part with Guy Clark (V24) and directly parallel to Rosanne Cash's own late-'80s Columbia records.

Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.description: Three guitarists trading melodic, chiming lines over motorik rhythms, with plainspoken, road-trip lyrics about growing up and moving on. It is one of the cleanest modern distillations of the Flying Nun/Go-Betweens jangle sound.
Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.lineage: Directly descended from Flying Nun-style Antipodean jangle-pop (The Clean, The Go-Betweens); part of the 2010s Australian guitar-pop wave alongside The Goon Sax and Twerps.

Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.description: A sunnier, more confident sequel to Hope Downs, with the same three-guitar interlock but bigger choruses and warmer production. Written partly about touring and homesickness.
Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.lineage: Second-generation Flying Nun-indebted jangle-pop, continuing the band's refinement of the sound.

Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.description: A darker, more expansive record with longer song structures and heavier guitar tones layered under the band's signature jangle. Terry rated it among the strongest guitar-pop records of 2022.
Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.lineage: Shows the band stretching its Flying Nun-descended jangle sound toward denser, more textured arrangements.

Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.description: The Melbourne trio's debut EP sets out the template their albums would follow: three guitarists trading tightly interlocked jangling lines over driving, motorik rhythms. Five songs of unpretentious, sun-bleached guitar pop that announced the band before Hope Downs.
Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.lineage: Grows out of the Go-Betweens/Triffids strand of Australian jangle-pop filtered through a more driving, Feelies-like guitar interplay.

Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.description: Their breakout EP, picked up by Sub Pop for US release, sharpens the interlocking three-guitar jangle of Talk Tight into tighter, more anthemic songs. It is the record that took the band from Melbourne club shows to international festival stages ahead of Hope Downs.
Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever.lineage: Bridges Talk Tight's homemade jangle-pop and the fuller, driving sound of Hope Downs, with the Feelies' interlocking-guitar template audible throughout.

Rosali.description: Rosali Middleman's early solo record pairs plainspoken, deceptively simple songwriting with restrained electric-guitar backing, patient rather than showy. It sets the template for her later work with David Nance's Mowed Sound band: songs that unravel slowly, revealing more with repeat listens.
Rosali.lineage: Rooted in the Philadelphia DIY folk scene, laying groundwork for her later collaborations with Nebraska's Mowed Sound band on No Medium and Bite Down.

Rosali.description: Rosali's first collaboration with David Nance's Mowed Sound band opens up her songs into looser, more guitar-forward arrangements, closer to Neil Young or Yo La Tengo than singer-songwriter folk. Josh Terry called it a standout of the decade.
Rosali.lineage: Marks the start of her ongoing partnership with the Mowed Sound band, a key thread connecting Philadelphia and Omaha DIY scenes.

Rosali.description: Rosali's fourth album and Merge Records debut, again with Nance's Mowed Sound band, elaborates elliptical folk songs into full-bodied guitar rock reminiscent of Yo La Tengo or Neil Young, while her voice carries the mesmerizing pull of Sandy Denny or Will Oldham.
Rosali.lineage: The full flowering of her Mowed Sound collaboration, moving her from DIY folk circles onto a larger indie label.

Rosanne Cash.description: Cash's breakthrough pairs her plainspoken, slightly weary alto with husband Rodney Crowell's rock-leaning production, and the title track (a number-one country hit that crossed onto the pop chart) sets the template: clean electric guitar, a steady rock backbeat, and lyrics that read like a diary entry rather than a Nashville formula song. My Baby Thinks He's a Train and Blue Moon with Heartache keep the same mix of honky-tonk twang and singer-songwriter directness, closer in spirit to the Eagles or Crowell's own records than to the countrypolitan mainstream. It made Cash one of the first artists to prove a rock-informed, gloss-averse country record could still top the country charts.
Rosanne Cash.lineage: Produced by Rodney Crowell out of the same Nashville songwriter circle as Guy Clark and Emmylou Harris (V24, V21), and its rock-informed but plainspoken sound sits at the commercial edge of this lane's country-rebel idea.

Rosanne Cash.description: King's Record Shop is Cash's most fully realized record, opening on the loping Rosie Strike Back and running through four number-one country singles including a cover of her father's Tennessee Flat Top Box reworked with a clean, ringing electric arrangement. The Way We Make a Broken Heart and If You Change Your Mind keep the same clear-eyed, unsentimental writing about failing relationships that ran through Seven Year Ache, now dressed in tighter, more confident production. It is generally rated her critical high point, the record where the rock-and-country hybrid she and Crowell had been refining since 1981 finally sounded effortless.
Rosanne Cash.lineage: The commercial and critical peak of Cash's Nashville-but-not-gloss run, directly continuing the sound of Seven Year Ache and closing out her most country-chart-facing period before her 1990s move toward rock (Interiors).

Rosanne Cash.description: Interiors strips away the rock-radio gloss of King's Record Shop almost entirely: Cash self-produced for the first time, working mostly with acoustic guitar, piano and minimal percussion behind unflinching songs about a marriage (her own, to Crowell) coming apart. On the Surface and What We Really Want trade in the earlier records' hooks for quiet, exposed confession, while I Want a Cure is as bleak as anything in her catalog. It effectively ended her run on the country charts but is now regarded as her most artistically serious record, the clearest break from Nashville's commercial expectations in her whole catalog.
Rosanne Cash.lineage: Marks Cash's decisive turn away from country radio toward singer-songwriter introspection, a move that foreshadows the plainspoken confessional songwriting later carried by V13's Americana songwriters.

Rose City Band.description: Ripley Johnson's (Wooden Shjips, Moon Duo) country-rock solo project debuts with seven warm, unhurried songs built on layered acoustic and electric guitars and Barry Walker's pedal steel. It trades Wooden Shjips' krautrock drone for direct, breezy homage to 1970s private-press country rock.
Rose City Band.lineage: Grew directly out of Johnson's psych-rock work in Wooden Shjips and Moon Duo, redirected toward Gram Parsons/Grateful Dead-style country rock; became a flagship of the 2020s cosmic-country revival.

Rose City Band.description: The second Rose City Band album widens the sound with fuller arrangements and a sunnier, more anthemic set of songs, still anchored by Johnson's laconic voice and Barry Walker's pedal steel. It plays like a long summer drive record, patient and glowing rather than showy.
Rose City Band.lineage: Expands on the debut's Gram Parsons/Grateful Dead-indebted template with a fuller studio sound.

Rose City Band.description: A patient, groove-heavy record that leans further into the band's live-jam reputation, with extended guitar and pedal-steel interplay over motorik rhythms. Fan reviews compare it to 'Wooden Shjips trading their sails for a prairie schooner' -- psychedelic country rock for a long, stoned drive.
Rose City Band.lineage: Continues Johnson's arc from Wooden Shjips' drone-rock toward fully-formed cosmic country.

Rose City Band.description: A tighter, hookier set than its predecessors, with standout single 'Mariposa' drawing praise from fans as an instant favorite. The band's core lineup (Johnson, Walker, Hasenberg, Jeffery) sound fully locked in, balancing sunlit pop songcraft with room to stretch out.
Rose City Band.lineage: Part of Rose City Band's steady evolution of the Gram Parsons/Grateful Dead cosmic-country template into a signature sound.

Rose City Band.description: Johnson's most emotionally shadowed Rose City Band record to date, letting a melancholy undertone sit alongside the band's usual sun-kissed grooves. Sanae Yamada (Moon Duo) guests on synths and vocals; Barry Walker's pedal steel remains the record's glinting through-line.
Rose City Band.lineage: The latest chapter in Johnson's long arc from Wooden Shjips/Moon Duo psych-drone to widescreen cosmic country.

Rosie Flores.description: Fresh from LA cowpunk band the Screamin' Sirens, Rosie Flores goes solo for a major-label debut that plays it straighter than her punk-scene work, rockabilly and honky-tonk delivered with a strong, unaffected country voice. The single "Crying Over You" gave her a minor chart hit and made her one of the few women from the cowpunk scene to cross into mainstream country radio, if only briefly. It is a late, straggling record in this lane, showing where a Hollywood cowpunk veteran landed once the scene's original energy started to fade.
Rosie Flores.lineage: A direct continuation of Flores' time in the Screamin' Sirens; her rockabilly-revival solo career afterward made her a recurring presence on reissue labels serving the alt-country audience of the 1990s.

Royal Trux.description: One of Drag City's earliest and most extreme releases, this double LP by Neil Hagerty and Jennifer Herrema buries whatever songs exist under tape hiss, guitar skronk and disorienting studio collage, closer to noise art than rock music. It is not deadpan-country in the Berman/Oldham sense, but it established Drag City's tolerance for uncompromising, DIY-damaged records and its co-founder Dan Koretzky credited the band with pushing 'everyone who listened' to reach beyond their grasp. Essential context for the label's identity even for listeners who find it unlistenable on first pass.
Royal Trux.lineage: The most extreme early Drag City release, documented as a direct influence on the label's willingness to release difficult, uncommercial records by the deadpan songwriters who followed, including Silver Jews and Smog.

Royal Trux.description: A comparatively more accessible record than Twin Infinitives, Cats and Dogs still buries Neil Hagerty and Jennifer Herrema's classic-rock bones under grime and distortion, with Hagerty's cracked, drawled vocals pushed low against overdriven guitars. It is often cited as the point where Royal Trux's damaged-rock-and-roll songwriting became legible under the noise. A useful reference point for the noisier, punk-adjacent edge of the Drag City roster.
Royal Trux.lineage: Follows Twin Infinitives as a slightly more song-oriented record, part of the same early Drag City catalog as the label's first Silver Jews and Smog releases, though pursuing a rock-damaged noise aesthetic rather than plainspoken songwriting.

Royal Trux.description: Royal Trux's major-label debut trades some of the earlier records' noise for a leaner, riff-based classic-rock sound closer to the Rolling Stones and Faces than to Drag City's other lo-fi records, though Hagerty and Herrema's ragged, drawled vocals stay just as unpolished. It is the record that made the band's underlying songcraft most obvious to outside listeners. Recommended for listeners curious how the Drag City noise wing connected to mainstream classic rock.
Royal Trux.lineage: Shows the classic-rock songwriting under the noise of the early Drag City records becoming explicit after a move to Virgin, before the band returned to Drag City for Accelerator and Veterans of Disorder.

Royal Trux.description: Royal Trux's return to Drag City after their major-label run, Accelerator pushes toward a colder, more mechanical sound built around drum machines and processed guitar, a sharp turn from Thank You's classic-rock warmth. It is a harder, more abrasive record that shows the duo restlessly reinventing their sound even within the same handful of years. A key transitional record before the band's dissolution around 2000.
Royal Trux.lineage: Marks Royal Trux's return to Drag City and a swing back toward the noisier end of their sound, part of the same label ecosystem as the deadpan songwriters even as their own music stayed far from that style.

Royal Trux.description: The last studio album of Royal Trux's original run, Veterans of Disorder returns to a looser, more classic-rock-indebted sound than Accelerator, with sprawling guitar workouts and Hagerty and Herrema's trademark ragged vocal trade-offs. It closes out the band's most productive era before Hagerty and Herrema split up personally and professionally around 2000. A solid capstone for listeners tracing the full arc of the band's Drag City years.
Royal Trux.lineage: Closes the original run of Royal Trux albums on Drag City before the 2000s reunion era on other labels, ending a decade in which the band and the deadpan songwriters shared a label without sharing a sound.

Rubber Rodeo.description: Formed by Rhode Island School of Design students, Rubber Rodeo crosses new-wave synths and drum machines with pedal steel and Trish Milliken/Bob Holmes' close vocal harmonies, a combination frontman Holmes described as "a cross between Gene Autry and Devo." Scenic Views covers everything from Dolly Parton to Ennio Morricone alongside originals, its slick, synthetic production making it an outlier even within the cowpunk scene. It represents the New England, art-school wing of the same punk-meets-country impulse driving the LA and Austin bands.
Rubber Rodeo.lineage: An East Coast counterpart to the LA cowpunk scene, its new-wave/country hybrid is a stylistic cousin to acts like the dB's and an early example of drum-machine country later echoed in alt-country's more experimental corners.

Ruby of Thanks.album: Before You Turn Into a Dog
Ruby of Thanks.description: Andy Weaver (drummer for Widowspeak, Castanets and his own band Wildflower) records intimate, handmade songs at home under the name Ruby of Thanks. Before You Turn Into a Dog values process over polish, preserving first-take performances of songs about love, work and finding peace.
Ruby of Thanks.lineage: Sits squarely in the Woodsist-orbit lo-fi home-recording tradition (Little Wings, John Andrews and the Yawns, Hand Habits), which itself descends from the DIY home-taping network.

Rui Gabriel.description: The solo debut from a member of a band Terry describes as splitting the difference between sing-along power pop and bracing post-punk, using a lighter palette of fun grooves and Summerteeth-grade hooks to write self-aware songs about class and miscommunication.
Rui Gabriel.lineage: A solo power-pop outlet indebted to Wilco's Summerteeth-era studio pop, signed to Carpark alongside label mates like Speedy Ortiz.

Russ Tolman.description: True West co-founder Russ Tolman's first solo album is a plainspoken, guitar-driven country-rock record, praised on release by New York Times critic Robert Palmer as a rock album of the week. 'Vegas' and 'Palm Tree Land' trade True West's guitar noise for cleaner, more directly narrative songwriting about Western landscapes and small lives. It shows one of the scene's guitarists moving toward the singer-songwriter Americana that the Paisley Underground fed into.
Russ Tolman.lineage: Made after Tolman stepped back from True West, carrying that band's Davis-scene, country-inflected guitar rock into a quieter solo format that anticipates the alt-country singer-songwriter wave of the following decade.

Ruston Kelly.description: Ruston Kelly's debut coined his own "dirt emo" tag: confessional, downcast lyrics about addiction and heartbreak set over pedal steel and plainspoken country-rock arrangements, closer in mood to emo than to Music Row polish. It moves between hushed acoustic laments and fuller, rootsy full-band tracks without losing its diary-like intimacy. It is a gateway record for listeners coming to alt-country from indie/emo rather than from classic country.
Ruston Kelly.lineage: Draws on Nashville's neo-traditional and outlaw country vocabulary but bends it toward emo's confessional mode, a hybrid Kelly himself named "dirt emo" and one later picked up across indie-adjacent country songwriting.

Rusty Wier.album: Don't It Make You Wanna Dance?
Rusty Wier.description: Rusty Wier's best-known album is built for a Saturday-night dancehall crowd, the title track (later a bigger hit for Bonnie Raitt-adjacent bar bands and a country radio staple) driven by a hard-strummed electric guitar and Wier's raspy, good-time shout. It stays close to the honky-tonk-meets-rock energy of the Armadillo World Headquarters crowd rather than the more introspective songwriting of Townes Van Zandt or Guy Clark. Wier was a fixture of the Austin scene's rowdier, bar-band side throughout the 1970s.
Rusty Wier.lineage: Represents the dancehall, bar-band end of the Austin cosmic-cowboy scene alongside Jerry Jeff Walker's Lost Gonzo Band and Michael Martin Murphey's early records.

Ryan Adams.description: Adams's solo debut after Whiskeytown is a spare, largely acoustic breakup record, cut quickly with guests like Emmylou Harris and Kim Richey. Songs like 'Come Pick Me Up' and 'Oh My Sweet Carolina' pair plainspoken heartbreak with a loose, unpolished feel closer to a demo tape than a studio product. It set the template for the prolific, genre-roaming solo career that followed.
Ryan Adams.lineage: Grew directly out of Whiskeytown's alt-country lineage, released on the same Bloodshot Records roster that carried the Old 97's and Waco Brothers.

Ryan Adams.description: A bigger, more classic-rock-indebted record than Heartbreaker, moving from the ballad 'When the Stars Go Blue' to the Stones-inflected 'New York, New York'. It broadened Adams's audience well beyond alt-country while still carrying pedal steel and country phrasing in places. The record's release date, days after September 11, and the accompanying video shot at the World Trade Center site, tied it to a specific cultural moment.
Ryan Adams.lineage: Shows Adams pulling further from Whiskeytown's twang toward mainstream rock, on the newly launched Lost Highway Records that would define much of 2000s alt-country and Americana.

Ryan Adams.description: Assembled from several shelved albums Adams recorded around this period, Demolition is a patchwork rather than a single session, but it holds together as a document of his mid-career restlessness. Songs range from gentle acoustic laments to full-band rockers, reflecting the different sessions they were pulled from. It is treated as a canonical part of his catalog rather than a stopgap rarities set.
Ryan Adams.lineage: Continues the singer-songwriter thread from Heartbreaker while showing Adams's growing pull toward rock, both released on Lost Highway during his most productive stretch.

Ryan Adams.description: The first record billed with backing band the Cardinals leans into extended, Grateful Dead-indebted jamming and pedal steel, spread across a double album. 'Magnolia Mountain' and 'Let It Ride' show a looser, more improvisational side of Adams than his earlier solo records. It reoriented his sound around a full band rather than a singer-songwriter frame.
Ryan Adams.lineage: Draws on the Cosmic American Music lineage of Gram Parsons and the Grateful Dead's country-rock wing, filtered through the same Lost Highway roster that housed Lucinda Williams and Old 97's.

Ryan Adams.description: Released the same year as Cold Roses, this is Adams's most straightforwardly honky-tonk record, cut with the Cardinals and featuring a duet with Norah Jones. Songs like 'The End' lean on classic country structure and pedal steel rather than the jam-band stretch of its sibling release. It is often cited by fans as his purest country album.
Ryan Adams.lineage: A direct nod to the Bakersfield and honky-tonk lineage the wider V zone traces back to, filtered through Adams's 2000s Lost Highway period alongside Jacksonville, NC roots he grew up with.

Ryan Adams.description: The third and least commercial of Adams's 2005 trilogy, a moodier, more sprawling record built around long, loosely structured songs rather than tight singles. It closes out an extraordinarily prolific year with a quieter, more introspective tone than Cold Roses or Jacksonville City Nights. Critics at the time treated it as a comedown after the other two, though it has aged into a cult favorite.
Ryan Adams.lineage: Caps Adams's remarkable 2005 run of three full-length albums on Lost Highway, all drawing on different corners of the alt-country and country-rock lineage.

Ryan Adams.description: A tighter, more polished record made after Adams got sober, trading the sprawl of 2005 for concise, hook-driven songs like 'Two' and 'Halloweenhead'. It is closer to power-pop and mainstream rock than to straight country, though pedal steel and twangy guitar leads still run through it. It became one of his more commercially successful post-Whiskeytown records.
Ryan Adams.lineage: Shows the pop-leaning endpoint of Adams's mid-2000s evolution away from strict alt-country, still released on the Lost Highway roster that anchored the genre's major-label wing.

Ryan Adams.description: A quiet, largely acoustic record made after a period away from music for health reasons, produced by Glyn Johns with Benmont Tench on piano. Songs like 'Come Home' return to the plainspoken intimacy of Heartbreaker after the louder detours of the mid-2000s. It reads as a settling-down record, both musically and personally.
Ryan Adams.lineage: Closes the loop back to Heartbreaker's spare singer-songwriter sound after a decade of genre experiments, marking the end of Adams's Lost Highway-era alt-country run before his major-label pop pivot.

Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.description: A sprawling seven-song double LP of conversational barfly rock, Davis half-sings dense, punning verses over a loose Roadhouse Band arrangement that folds pedal steel and violin into synths and programmed beats. It is dark, funny and grand at once, with guest harmonies from Will Oldham, Catherine Irwin and Lou Turner deepening its Drag City-indebted, David Berman-adjacent lineage. For listeners who want the modern high-water mark of wordy, tragicomic songwriting.
Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.lineage: Davis fronted the earlier Louisville band State Champion before going solo with the Roadhouse Band; the record extends the Silver Jews/David Berman line of deadpan storytelling into the 2020s.

Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.description: Davis's first billed Roadhouse Band record, a 2-LP set of seven expansive, mostly 6-plus-minute songs that mix folk-traditioned wordplay with synth textures, organ swells and pedal steel. Joan Shelley and Freakwater's Catherine Irwin guest, and the mood is melancholic and gentle rather than rowdy. A good entry point for the barfly-poet strain of the scene before New Threats from the Soul refined it further.
Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.lineage: Follows Davis's work fronting State Champion and Tropical Trash; draws explicitly on Souled American, David Berman and Neil Young comparisons per the label's own description.

Ryley Walker.description: Walker's breakthrough backs his fingerpicked-guitar songwriting with Chicago jazz and experimental players (including cellist/improviser Fred Lonberg-Holm), stretching folk songs into loose, Van Morrison-and-Tim Buckley-indebted jams. It is warm, exploratory and unhurried.
Ryley Walker.lineage: Grew out of Walker's Chicago DIY cassette-EP years, pulling jazz improvisation into a folk-rock frame indebted to Astral Weeks and the Grateful Dead's more pastoral side.

Ryley Walker.album: Golden Sings That Have Been Sung
Ryley Walker.description: A deliberate evolution from Primrose Green's jazz-folk sprawl toward tighter, more song-focused arrangements, still built on Walker's intricate guitar work and a loose, breezy band feel. Reviewers noted it as 'yet another change' in his continually shifting sound.
Ryley Walker.lineage: The second of Walker's Dead Oceans albums, part of his restless movement between folk, jazz and rock idioms.

Ryley Walker.description: A deliberately harder-to-parse record than Walker's earlier Fahey-descended solo-guitar albums, Deafman Glance buries anti-folk songwriting under synths, warped studio effects and Chicago free-improv contributors like Cooper Crain and Nate Lepine. Walker has called it a record for 'coming up or coming down.'
Ryley Walker.lineage: Walker's most experimental studio record, pulling his American Primitive guitar roots into Chicago's free-improv and noise scene.

S.G. Goodman.description: Kentucky songwriter S.G. Goodman's debut is a rocking, rootsy country-folk record steeped in her rural western-Kentucky upbringing, connected with My Morning Jacket's Jim James, who produced it. Tyler Childers later covered its song 'Space and Time.' A stark, plainspoken start to Goodman's catalog.
S.G. Goodman.lineage: Sits alongside Tyler Childers and Ian Noe in the western-Kentucky storyteller wing of the new country scene, sharing Childers' own admiration and later cover of her material.

S.G. Goodman.description: Goodman's second album sharpens her rural-Kentucky storytelling into a bleaker, more electric record about depression and rural isolation, earning her the Americana Music Association's Emerging Artist of the Year award. The arrangements lean harder into fuzzy guitar than her debut without losing its plainspoken drawl. A more confident, harder-hitting follow-up.
S.G. Goodman.lineage: Extends Old Time Feeling's western-Kentucky storytelling into darker territory, part of the same post-Childers Kentucky scene as Ian Noe.

S.G. Goodman.description: Goodman's third album, released on her own Slough Water Records with Thirty Tigers, turns toward the folk-magic and planting traditions of her rural Kentucky community for its imagery. It keeps the plainspoken, rootsy sound of her earlier records while widening its spiritual and agricultural language. A settled, personal record from one of the scene's most distinctive Kentucky voices.
S.G. Goodman.lineage: Continues Goodman's western-Kentucky storytelling lineage on her own label imprint, tying her catalog directly to the region's folk traditions.

Sadurn.description: Genevieve DeGroot's full-band debut, recorded in a Poconos cabin during the pandemic; spare, diary-like indie folk indebted to Jason Molina, Gillian Welch and Elliott Smith.
Sadurn.lineage: Grew from DeGroot's lo-fi Philadelphia DIY EPs into a full four-piece band; part of the Philly indie-folk scene alongside Pearla and Greg Mendez.

Saintseneca.description: Recorded with Mike Mogis in Omaha after signing to ANTI-, Dark Arc pairs the band's dulcimer-and-mandolin folk instrumentation with denser, more electric production.
Saintseneca.lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

Saintseneca.description: A pop-structured folk-rock record built on the band's trademark mix of banjo, dulcimer and balalaika alongside synths and electric guitars.
Saintseneca.lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

Saintseneca.description: An unexpected, innovative folk-rock record per NPR, mixing Appalachian string-band instrumentation with contemporary electronic touches.
Saintseneca.lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

Saintseneca.description: Saintseneca's first album in seven years, produced by Steve Ciolek, full of heady surrealist lyrics and rousing, off-kilter earworm hooks.
Saintseneca.lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

Salem 66.description: Salem 66's third album pairs the twin vocals of Judy Grunwald and Beth Kaplan over ringing, mid-tempo guitar rock, part of Homestead Records' Boston-area roster. It leans folkier and more melodic than the label's noisier acts, with plainspoken lyrics and close, conversational harmonies. A representative slice of American underground/college-rock's gentler wing.
Salem 66.lineage: Boston Homestead-label peers of Dinosaur Jr. and Salem 66's own earlier work with Sonic Youth's Lee Ranaldo producing; part of the SST/Homestead college-radio network that fed the later lo-fi and Bandcamp DIY scene.

Sam Amidon.description: Amidon's first Nonesuch album, produced by longtime collaborator Thomas Bartlett, reworks old-time and traditional songs (its title track a Civil War-era ballad) into spare, occasionally jazz-inflected arrangements built around his plain, unhurried voice and banjo. Raised by folk-revival parents and steeped in the Harry Smith Anthology as a teenager, Amidon treats old songs as raw material to be reshaped rather than preserved. A good entry point for listeners who want old-time source material filtered through an experimental indie-folk sensibility.
Sam Amidon.lineage: Extends the Anthology of American Folk Music tradition into 2010s indie folk, sharing Nonesuch's roster with Gillian Welch and drawing on the same song-collecting impulse behind Jake Xerxes Fussell's records.

Sam Blasucci.description: Mapache's Sam Blasucci steps out solo, trading intertwined acoustic guitars for a piano his bandmate's mother gave away, writing fully autobiographical songs about settling into adult life. Covers of Dido's 'Thank You' and the Cranberries' 'Linger' sit unironically alongside the originals.
Sam Blasucci.lineage: A solo detour from Mapache's California cosmic-country duo sound, recorded with Mapache collaborator Johnny Payne at Dan Horne's Lone Palm Studio.

Sam Blasucci.description: Blasucci's third solo LP, an airy, piano-led set that trades some of Off My Stars' folk directness for a more sophisticated pop croon, with contributions from Andres Renteria, Mia Wilson and Laena Myers. Tasteful rather than showy, it continues his move away from Mapache's guitar-forward sound.
Sam Blasucci.lineage: Follows Off My Stars and the glam-pop Real Life Thing in Blasucci's ongoing solo evolution away from Mapache's duo format.

Sam Burton.base: Los Angeles, CA (via Salt Lake City)
Sam Burton.description: Burton's debut LP, produced by Jarvis Taveniere of Woods, pairs a high, Roy Orbison-like wail with moody, echo-laden country-rock production. The L.A. Times called it 'an old, weird Americana sound filled with echo and longing' -- timeless rather than retro.
Sam Burton.lineage: Produced by Woods' Jarvis Taveniere, tying Burton directly into the Woodsist/cosmic-country lineage; released on Tompkins Square, the American Primitive-adjacent folk label.

Sam Burton.description: Burton's second album trades some of I Can Go With You's stark folk for fuller, Laurel Canyon-style arrangements, with pedal steel and strings framing his warm, unhurried baritone. It's gentler and more polished than the debut without losing its plainspoken sadness.
Sam Burton.lineage: Moves Burton from the Tompkins Square country-folk revival roster toward a wider, Nashville-adjacent take on '70s soft country rock.

Sam Evian.description: Sam Owens' debut as Sam Evian is a warm, lightly psychedelic bedroom-folk record, its analog haze pointing toward the Flying Cloud studio he'd later build with Hannah Cohen. It's an older record Terry has singled out in show recaps as a formative favorite.
Sam Evian.lineage: The starting point for the Flying Cloud/Hannah Cohen upstate-New York recording circle Evian would go on to anchor as a producer.

Sam Evian.description: Sam Owens's fourth album as Sam Evian was tracked live to vintage tape over ten days with Adrianne Lenker and El Kempner guesting, chasing a warm, early-1970s Laurel Canyon feel across nine loose, groove-driven songs about his parents' relationship.
Sam Evian.lineage: A Catskills singer-songwriter working in the Laurel Canyon/Gram Parsons-adjacent cosmic-country lineage, produced at his own Flying Cloud Studios alongside Big Thief collaborators.

Sam Moss.description: A raspy-voiced, earthy folk record featuring players from Califone, Megafaun, Mountain Goats and Mountain Man; Nathan Salsburg calls it Moss's best yet.
Sam Moss.lineage: New England-born, Virginia-based guitarist whose fingerstyle folk draws on the same Appalachian/American Primitive lineage as Jake Xerxes Fussell.

Sam Outlaw.description: Outlaw's debut is smooth, Southern-California country in the Bakersfield/Palomino Club tradition, produced with a warm, string-laced sheen rather than rough honky-tonk grit. It's more countrypolitan than outlaw despite the stage name. A pleasant, LA-scene counterpart to the rowdier Texas and Kentucky wings of the lane.
Sam Outlaw.lineage: Draws on the Southern California country tradition of Buck Owens and the Bakersfield sound as filtered through LA's contemporary Americana scene.

Sam Outlaw.description: Outlaw's second album keeps the same smooth Southern California country sound while leaning further into string-laced ballads and romantic songwriting. It's a comfortable rather than adventurous follow-up. A steady entry for fans of the LA countrypolitan wing of the scene.
Sam Outlaw.lineage: Continues the same Bakersfield-by-way-of-LA countrypolitan lineage established on Angeleno.

Sammi Smith.album: Help Me Make It Through the Night
Sammi Smith.description: Sammi Smith's smoky, unhurried reading of the title track, a Kris Kristofferson song, became a crossover hit and won the CMA Award for Single of the Year, turning a little-known Mega Records singer into one of outlaw country's few prominent female voices. The rest of the album leans on the same behind-the-beat, late-night phrasing, closer to a smoky bar than a Nashville showcase. It is a key document of how Kristofferson's songwriting reached listeners years before his own albums did.
Sammi Smith.lineage: Built around a Kris Kristofferson song recorded before his own version reached wide audiences, tying Smith's career directly to the outlaw movement's key songwriter.

Sandy Bull.description: Recorded two years before Fahey's Transfiguration, Bull's debut pairs a side-long banjo arrangement of Carl Orff's Carmina Burana with a side of oud- and raga-inflected electric guitar, making it one of the earliest records to treat American folk instruments as vehicles for modal, non-Western improvisation. It predates and runs parallel to the Takoma scene rather than descending from it, drawing on jazz and world music as much as blues. Its scale and ambition mark it as a founding text of guitar-based drone music.
Sandy Bull.lineage: An early, largely independent forerunner of American Primitive guitar's raga and drone side, closer in spirit to Robbie Basho than to Fahey, and a clear ancestor of the long-form instrumental pieces later made by Marisa Anderson and Chuck Johnson.

Sandy Denny.album: The North Star Grassman and the Ravens
Sandy Denny.description: Sandy Denny's debut solo album after leaving Fotheringay pairs her own increasingly personal songwriting, especially the elegiac 'Late November' and the war-haunted 'John the Gun,' with covers of Brenda's 'Down in the Flood' and the traditional 'Blackwaterside.' Her old Fairport bandmates and members of Fotheringay back her, so the sound stays close to electric folk-rock even as the album is billed as a solo statement. It set the pattern for her run of solo records through the mid-1970s.
Sandy Denny.lineage: Follows directly from Fotheringay's breakup and keeps Denny's songwriting in the same Fairport-adjacent folk-rock lineage that later solo albums Sandy and Like an Old Fashioned Waltz continued.

Sandy Denny.description: Denny's second solo album is more polished than her Fairport or Fotheringay work, with string and horn arrangements framing 'Listen, Listen' and 'The Lady,' plus a cover of Dylan's 'Tomorrow Is a Long Time.' Her voice carries the record: full, aching, and precise on both her own compositions and the traditional 'Bushes and Briars.' It is generally ranked among her strongest solo statements and a high point of the Island folk-rock roster she came up through.
Sandy Denny.lineage: Continues the Fairport-and-Fotheringay folk-rock sound in a more orchestrated, singer-songwriter direction that influenced later British female singer-songwriters.

Sandy Denny.description: Denny's third solo album pushes further into orchestrated pop and cabaret, with a Cliff Richard duet on 'Whispering Grass' sitting alongside the stark 'At the End of the Day' and 'No End,' one of the bleakest things she recorded. It sold poorly and marked the point where Island's patience with her solo career was running out. The record is less often cited than her Fairport-era work but shows her range past straight folk-rock.
Sandy Denny.lineage: The least folk-rock of Denny's solo run, pulled toward orchestral pop, though it still follows directly from Sandy and The North Star Grassman and the Ravens.

Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.description: Shook's debut with the Disarmers is a raw, high-lonesome blend of honky-tonk twang and punk attitude, cut live at a North Carolina studio with pedal steel and fiddle behind a defiantly unpolished voice. Songs about bad relationships, drinking and small-town claustrophobia sit in the same unglamorous, storytelling tradition as the wider Southern rock scene, though delivered by a quartet rather than a three-guitar band. It built a regional reputation that led Bloodshot Records to re-release the album in 2017.
Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.lineage: Grew out of Shook's earlier, short-lived bands Sarah Shook and the Devil and Sarah Shook and the Dirty Hands in the Chapel Hill, NC scene, and its cowpunk twang connects it to both the Drive-By Truckers-descended storytelling lane and the Bloodshot Records alt-country network.

Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.description: Shook's Bloodshot Records debut sharpens the vocal control while keeping the same defiant, high-lonesome twang, with the Rolling Stone-praised 'Good as Gold' showing a crisper, more controlled delivery than Sidelong's rawer sound. The band toured heavily while writing it, and the road-worn tightness shows in the arrangements. It extended Shook's reputation as one of the sharper voices in the Bloodshot stable of outlaw-leaning country acts.
Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.lineage: A direct follow-up to Sidelong on Bloodshot Records, the Chicago label that also carried Two Cow Garage-adjacent acts and the wider insurgent-country scene Drive-By Truckers emerged from.

Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.description: Delayed by the sale of Bloodshot Records and eventually released on Thirty Tigers, this album was produced by Dwight Yoakam collaborator Pete Anderson and brings in organ alongside the returning pedal steel. It keeps Shook's defiant, plainspoken honky-tonk songwriting intact while sounding fuller and more countrypolitan than the earlier records. The lineup shuffle around it, with drummer Will Rigby joining, marks a more stable full-band era for the group.
Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.lineage: Continues the honky-tonk-and-punk sound of Sidelong and Years under a new label home after Bloodshot's 2020 sale, produced by veteran Bakersfield-sound engineer Pete Anderson.

Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.description: Released as River Shook publicly affirmed their non-binary identity, this record keeps the band's honky-tonk-and-punk core while turning its plainspoken storytelling toward self-acceptance and reinvention. It is a more settled, confident-sounding record than the earlier albums, without losing the band's defiant edge. It shows a decade-plus band still finding new personal territory within the same outlaw-country-adjacent sound.
Sarah Shook & the Disarmers.lineage: The most recent Disarmers album on Thirty Tigers, continuing the honky-tonk-punk sound established on Sidelong within the same Chapel Hill, NC-rooted band.

Say Sue Me.description: A Busan band's debut full-length, applying warm, ringing jangle-pop guitar tones to plainspoken, sea-town songwriting; the start of a consistently pristine throwback indie-rock run.
Say Sue Me.lineage: Descends from Flying Nun/Byrds-style jangle-pop transplanted to the Korean indie scene.

Say Sue Me.description: Terry cites this as the start of the band's run of great, pristine throwback indie rock: sun-bleached, reverb-drenched jangle-pop that recalls the Byrds by way of Real Estate.
Say Sue Me.lineage: Continuation of Say Sue Me's Flying Nun/Byrds-descended jangle-pop songwriting.

Say Sue Me.description: Self-recorded and self-produced during lockdown at the Busan band's own studio, this is Say Sue Me's most inward record, built around themes of self-love and realization rather than the surf-jangle bounce of earlier singles. Guest spots from Korean jazz musicians Kim Ildu and Kim Oki widen the palette without losing the band's pristine, throwback jangle-pop core.
Say Sue Me.lineage: Continues the Busan band's pristine, Alvvays-adjacent throwback indie-pop songwriting, turning inward after Where We Were Together's touring cycle.

Scott H. Biram.album: The Dirty Old One Man Band
Scott H. Biram.description: Biram plays every instrument himself on this raw, distorted mix of blues, punk, and honky-tonk, recorded with heavy amp distortion that makes even acoustic country songs sound like they came off a garage-punk record. His hollering, road-worn voice sits over stomping one-man-band arrangements. It was his first release for Bloodshot Records after surviving a near-fatal car accident.
Scott H. Biram.lineage: Applies Bloodshot's insurgent-country ethos to a solo one-man-band format, closer to punk-blues than to any conventional country arrangement.

Scott H. Biram.description: Continuing his one-man-band assault of distorted blues, honky-tonk, and gospel, Biram keeps the raw, lo-fi production of his debut for Bloodshot while sharpening the songwriting. Tracks alternate between full-throated punk-blues stompers and quieter, more traditional country moments. It cemented his reputation as one of the rawest acts on the Bloodshot roster.
Scott H. Biram.lineage: Extends Biram's fusion of Delta blues, honky-tonk, and punk energy, showing the rougher, punk-adjacent edge of the Bloodshot roster's insurgent-country umbrella.

Scott H. Biram.description: A slightly more varied record than his earliest Bloodshot releases, still built on Biram's solo one-man-band setup but stretching further into gospel and metal-adjacent heaviness at points. His voice remains a ragged, shouted instrument as much as a singing one. It continued his steady, prolific output on Bloodshot Records.
Scott H. Biram.lineage: Keeps Biram's punk-blues-gospel hybrid within the Bloodshot roster, a rougher counterpart to the label's more straightforwardly twangy acts.

Scout Niblett.description: An English songwriter who joined Drag City for her fifth album, Niblett strips her songs down to just guitar or piano and drums, alternating between a flat, deadpan murmur and sudden shouted outbursts. The extreme minimalism and raw emotional swings fit naturally alongside the label's other stripped-down, plainspoken records even though her delivery is rawer and more volatile than Berman's or Oldham's. A useful record for hearing how the Drag City aesthetic extended to a very different, more confrontational British songwriter.
Scout Niblett.lineage: Niblett's move to Drag City for this album connects her raw, minimal singer-songwriter style to the label's broader deadpan-adjacent roster, extending the sound to a harder-edged British voice.

Scout Niblett.description: Niblett's second and final Drag City album keeps the same stark guitar/drums or piano/drums format as her prior record, working through a breakup with the same mix of flat delivery and sudden vocal eruptions. Steve Albini-adjacent production values (spare, room-heavy drum sound) keep the focus on the raw performance rather than studio polish. A logical next step for listeners who start with The Calcination of Scout Niblett.
Scout Niblett.lineage: Closes out Niblett's run on Drag City, continuing the raw, minimal singer-songwriter approach that linked her to the label's other stripped-down artists.

Scrawl.description: Scrawl's second album is rough, unglamorous Midwestern guitar rock led by Marcy Mays' and Sue Harshe's plainspoken, alternately deadpan and shouted vocals. The playing is loose and live-sounding, closer to a bar band than a studio project, with blunt lyrics about drinking and bad relationships. A rawer, more female-fronted counterpart to labelmates like the Replacements.
Scrawl.lineage: Columbus, Ohio underground contemporaries of Great Plains; part of the same Homestead/Rough Trade-era college-rock network that fed the '90s slacker and lo-fi scenes.

Screamin' Sirens.description: An all-female Hollywood band featuring future rockabilly solo artist Rosie Flores, the Screamin' Sirens mix country, rockabilly and punk into what drummer Boom Boom Laffoon described wanting to sound like a wild, gang-like all-girl band. Fiesta! plays fast and unpolished, delivered in cowboy boots and western skirts on stage, part of the same Hollywood club circuit as Tex & the Horseheads and Blood on the Saddle. It is a good document of the scene's rowdier, more punk-tempo end.
Screamin' Sirens.lineage: Part of the second wave of LA cowpunk bands that formed after X and the Blasters opened the door; Rosie Flores' presence directly ties the band to her own subsequent rockabilly solo career.

Screaming Trees.description: A more classic-rock-tinged entry from the eastern-Washington band, pairing Mark Lanegan's deep baritone with psychedelic, Crazy Horse-adjacent guitar work. Its blend of grunge heaviness and '60s/'70s rock songcraft made it a critical favorite that never matched its peers' sales.
Screaming Trees.lineage: A Crazy Horse-tinged outlier within X8's Seattle scene, closer in guitar tone to V20 than to punk-rooted grunge, though its commercial path still runs through '90s alt radio rather than the Core.

Scud Mountain Boys.description: Joe Pernice's plainspoken drawl narrates small-town New England scenes over quiet, pedal-steel-laced country-rock played so slowly it borders on lullaby tempo, a deliberate reaction against the band's earlier, rowdier bar-band sound. The production is intimate and unhurried, closer to a living-room session than a studio record, letting Pernice's storytelling songwriting sit front and center. It is widely regarded as the band's masterpiece and a key transitional record between No Depression-style alt-country and the hushed, sadder register of slowcore.
Scud Mountain Boys.lineage: Sits at the intersection of alt-country storytelling and slowcore's quiet dynamics, a direct bridge between the V9 insurgent-country scene and V12's hushed sadness; Pernice would go on to the more pop-oriented Pernice Brothers.

Scud Mountain Boys.description: This Massachusetts band's debut is a hushed, largely acoustic record of plainspoken heartbreak songs, closer in spirit to a barroom last call than to the louder cowpunk bands of the same moment. Joe Pernice's flat, weary voice and the band's unhurried tempos gave the Northeast its own quiet answer to the twangier Midwest and Texas scenes. A key document of New England's contribution to 1990s insurgent country.
Scud Mountain Boys.lineage: Part of the same small-club Northampton, Massachusetts scene that produced Dinosaur Jr. and the Pixies' extended circle, applying that region's DIY ethic to a hushed, pedal-steel version of insurgent country.

Sea Level.description: Sea Level formed when Allman Brothers pianist Chuck Leavell, bassist Lamar Williams, and drummer Jai Johanny Johanson began jamming during the Allmans' mid-1970s hiatus, adding guitarist Jimmy Nalls for a jazzier, more fusion-leaning spinoff of the Allmans' sound. Leavell's piano, already famous from his solo on the Allmans' 'Jessica,' carries most of the record's melodic weight across songs like 'Rain in Spain' and a lengthy instrumental cover of 'Scarborough Fair.' It traded some of the Allmans' blues grit for a lighter, more virtuosic jazz-rock feel, aimed at the same Capricorn audience.
Sea Level.lineage: Formed by Allman Brothers Band members Chuck Leavell, Lamar Williams, and Jai Johanny Johanson during the Allmans' 1976 breakup, Sea Level is a direct Capricorn Records offshoot of the flagship band's sound.

Seam.description: Formed by former Bitch Magnet guitarist Sooyoung Park after relocating from Chapel Hill to Chicago, Seam's debut pairs slow, deliberate tempos with hushed vocals that occasionally give way to walls of guitar noise. It sits at the meeting point of slowcore and the era's noisier indie underground, patient where most of Seam's contemporaries were fast and loose. The record's restraint became the band's defining trait.
Seam.lineage: Sooyoung Park's post-Bitch Magnet project, moving from the Chapel Hill scene to Chicago and helping define the slowcore-adjacent, hushed-to-loud dynamic that ran alongside 1990s slacker rock.

Seam.description: Seam's Touch and Go debut refines the hushed-to-loud dynamic of Headsparks into more fully developed songs, with Sooyoung Park's flat vocal delivery sitting over slow, spacious arrangements that occasionally erupt into distortion. It is a patient, melancholy record that never rushes to make its point. The band's understated approach influenced a wide swath of the emo and slowcore scenes that followed.
Seam.lineage: Seam's move to Touch and Go Records deepened their hushed, deliberate sound, an approach that would go on to directly influence Midwest emo and slowcore bands through the rest of the decade.

Seam.description: Seam's third album keeps the patient, hushed pace of its predecessors while adding new drummer Chris Manfrin's steadier rhythmic backbone, giving the songs a slightly more grounded feel than the band's earlier work. Sooyoung Park's lyrics stay understated and interior, matching the unhurried music. It continued the band's quiet influence on the era's slowcore and emo undergrounds without ever seeking a wider audience.
Seam.lineage: Continues Seam's Touch and Go run of hushed, deliberate indie rock, part of the same Chicago underground that included Tortoise and other members of the post-Bitch Magnet, post-hardcore diaspora.

Sean Thompson's Weird Ears.description: Sean Thompson's first solo EP after years as a Nashville sideman, short and direct, exploring his own songwriting voice with a small backing band of drums, keys and bass. A modest but confident opening statement for the project.
Sean Thompson's Weird Ears.lineage: Grew out of Thompson's time in Nashville DIY bands (Gnarwhal, Promised Land Sound) before he became a touring guitarist for Margo Price and others.

Sean Thompson's Weird Ears.description: Thompson's debut full-band LP trades some of his earlier twang for exploratory, cosmic territory, with easygoing songs about country living and long drives. Josh Terry called him his favorite touring guitarist, previewing this as a step forward from the project's 2022 self-titled EP.
Sean Thompson's Weird Ears.lineage: Builds on Thompson's Nashville session career and his earlier Weird Ears EPs into a fuller cosmic-country-jam statement.

Sebadoh.description: Sebadoh III splits the difference between Lou Barlow's hushed four-track confessionals and Eric Gaffney's noisier, more abrasive experiments, with the two songwriters' fragments stacked back to back rather than smoothed into a single band sound. The record includes 'Freed Pig,' Barlow's blunt, deadpan kiss-off to his former band Dinosaur Jr. and bandmate J Mascis, alongside noisier collage pieces and hushed acoustic sketches. Its raw, unedited home-recording ethic became a reference point for the American lo-fi scene that followed.
Sebadoh.lineage: Grew out of Lou Barlow's home four-track recordings made after his acrimonious split from Dinosaur Jr., establishing Sebadoh as a defining lo-fi act alongside Guided by Voices and feeding directly into 'Bubble & Scrape' and the Sub Pop years.

Sebadoh.description: Sebadoh's Sub Pop debut keeps the four-track intimacy of the Homestead years but lets songs breathe a little longer, with 'Soul and Fire' pairing Lou Barlow's plainspoken vocal against ragged, minor-key guitar. Eric Gaffney's more chaotic contributions still puncture the record's quieter moments, keeping it from settling into polish. It is the transitional record between Sebadoh's cassette-culture beginnings and the tighter songwriting of 'Bakesale.'
Sebadoh.lineage: The first Sebadoh album for Sub Pop, carrying the band's Homestead-era four-track method onto a bigger indie platform and setting up the more focused songwriting of 'Bakesale.'

Sebadoh.description: 'Bakesale' is Sebadoh's most immediate record, Lou Barlow's songwriting sharpened into compact, hook-driven tracks like 'Skull' and 'Magnet's Coil' while keeping the thin, close-mic'd production of the band's earlier four-track work. Jason Loewenstein's rougher, punkier songs balance out Barlow's melodic streak across the record. It is often cited as the point where Sebadoh's lo-fi habits and pop instincts lined up most cleanly.
Sebadoh.lineage: Follows 'Bubble & Scrape' as Sebadoh's breakthrough on Sub Pop, tightening the band's four-track aesthetic into concise songs that widened their audience beyond the lo-fi underground.

Sebadoh.description: 'Harmacy' pushes Sebadoh toward fuller, more conventionally produced arrangements without losing Lou Barlow's plainspoken, heartbroken delivery, as on 'Ocean' and 'On Fire.' It still carries the band's home-recording DNA in its unpolished mixes and Jason Loewenstein's rawer songs, even as some tracks approach straightforward alt-rock. It marks the point where Sebadoh's sound had drifted furthest from its four-track cassette roots while still being recognizably the same band.
Sebadoh.lineage: The last Sebadoh album from the band's classic lineup era, closing out the run that began with the Homestead cassettes and carried through Sub Pop into more conventional studio recording.

Sebadoh.description: Sebadoh's debut stitches together Lou Barlow's four-track bedroom sketches with Eric Gaffney's noisier tape experiments and no real attempt to smooth the seams between them. Songs blur into short instrumental fragments and spoken-word snippets, closer to a mixtape of a songwriter's private archive than a produced album. It is rougher and less song-oriented than what followed, but it set the template of unedited home-tape collage that Sebadoh built a career on.
Sebadoh.lineage: Grew directly out of Lou Barlow's four-track recordings made in the wake of his split from Dinosaur Jr., and established the raw, unedited home-tape method that 'Weed Forestin'' and 'Sebadoh III' then refined.

Sebadoh.description: Recorded almost entirely by Lou Barlow alone on a four-track, 'Weed Forestin'' is quieter and more song-focused than the debut, with plainspoken confessional pieces sitting next to tape hiss and half-finished ideas. Barlow's voice stays close-mic'd and unguarded throughout, favoring mood and diary-like candor over polish. Later reissued alongside 'The Freed Man' material as 'The Freed Weed,' it remains a key document of Barlow's early solo four-track songwriting.
Sebadoh.lineage: The second Sebadoh full-length, deepening Lou Barlow's four-track home-recording method just before Eric Gaffney's contributions expanded on 'Sebadoh III.'

Sebadoh.album: Smash Your Head on the Punk Rock
Sebadoh.description: A compilation pulling together Sebadoh's scattered early singles, compilation tracks, and four-track ephemera from the Homestead years, 'Smash Your Head on the Punk Rock' is deliberately abrasive and unpolished even by the band's own low standards. It captures Eric Gaffney's noisier, more collage-based side as much as Lou Barlow's songwriting, with tape edits and abrupt cuts left audible. It stands as the era's most direct document of Sebadoh's pre-Sub Pop home-tape underground.
Sebadoh.lineage: Gathers early Homestead-era Sebadoh recordings into a single canonical document of the band's rawest four-track period, bridging 'Weed Forestin'' and 'Sebadoh III.'

Shabason & Krgovich.description: Four Days in June has Joseph Shabason and Nicholas Krgovich reaching for CD-era songcraft in the vein of Neil Young's Harvest Moon and k.d. lang, its brushed drums and understated pedal steel, banjo and fiddle (courtesy of guest Sam Amidon) giving their usual wry chamber-pop a country-rock glow.
Shabason & Krgovich.lineage: Named after Blue Rodeo's alt-country landmark Five Days in July, this record openly borrows from 90s pop-country and Cosmic American touchstones while keeping the duo's own understated, plainspoken songwriting.

Shallowater.description: Shallowater call themselves "raw West Texas dirtgaze," and this eight-song debut earns the tag: dusty, string-bent guitar figures get swallowed by walls of overdriven noise, with a drawled, half-buried vocal riding on top. It is a rougher, more indebted-to-shoegaze record than the band's later work, closer to noise rock with a country skeleton than to polished Americana.
Shallowater.lineage: Debut full-length that establishes the dirtgaze sound Shallowater expand on with God's Gonna Give You A Million Dollars; part of the small post-Wednesday wave of Texas and Southern bands mixing noise-rock scale with country phrasing.

Shallowater.album: God's Gonna Give You A Million Dollars
Shallowater.description: Six tracks over 41 minutes, several stretching past seven or eight minutes, swinging between ear-splitting guitar walls and glacial, delicate melodies. As Terry put it, the record swings between ear-splitting riffs and glacial, delicate melodies, and it is the fullest realization yet of the band's "dirtgaze" idea: country-song bones dressed in noise-rock scale.
Shallowater.lineage: Second Shallowater LP, expanding the noise/twang balance of There Is A Well into longer, more patient song structures; part of the same wave as Dutch Interior and Wednesday.

Shania Twain.description: Produced with then-husband Mutt Lange, Come On Over fused country storytelling with arena-pop and rock production (programmed drums, big guitar hooks) on hits like 'Man! I Feel Like a Woman!' and 'You're Still the One,' becoming the best-selling country album by a woman ever. It sanded away nearly all twang for maximal pop crossover appeal. It is for listeners tracing how far countrypolitan's pop instincts could travel before the genre line disappeared.
Shania Twain.lineage: Takes the pop-crossover ambitions of the countrypolitan lane (Glen Campbell, and later Garth Brooks's arena scale) to their commercial extreme, largely abandoning traditional instrumentation; its pop-first template anticipates the vocal-hook-driven side of 2010s mainstream country.

Shannon Lay.description: Released on Kevin Morby's Mare imprint, Living Water is a spare, Nick Drake-and-Vashti-Bunyan-indebted folk record built on close-mic'd guitar and Lay's airy voice.
Shannon Lay.lineage: Lay's second solo album, made between stints in the LA punk band Feels; part of the LA cosmic-folk revival around Ty Segall's circle.

Shannon Lay.description: Lay's first album as a full-time musician and first for Sub Pop, co-produced with Ty Segall and dressed with a wider array of instrumentation than her earlier records.
Shannon Lay.lineage: Marks Lay's move from Feels' punk records into a dedicated solo folk career.

Shannon Lay.description: Lay's fifth album, self-released on her own All the Best label, adds pedal steel, piano and synths to her folk core with a larger team of musicians than before.
Shannon Lay.lineage: Follows Geist and Covers Vol. 1 as Lay's most expansive solo record to date.

Sharon Van Etten.description: Van Etten's second album, made after leaving an emotionally controlling relationship, is stark and confessional, her voice cracking under the weight of the lyrics over mostly acoustic guitar. 'Peace Signs' and 'Save Yourself' read like direct diary entries rather than folk-narrative character studies, closer to early Cat Power than to Gillian Welch's borrowed old-time forms. It remains her rawest, least produced record before her sound expanded.
Sharon Van Etten.lineage: Plainspoken, guitar-and-voice confessional songwriting in the lineage of early Cat Power and Bill Callahan, recorded in the same lo-fi Brooklyn DIY circle that produced Julianna Barwick and Grizzly Bear.

Sharon Van Etten.description: Produced by the National's Aaron Dessner and recorded piecemeal in his Brooklyn basement studio, Tramp brings in guest vocalists from the National, Beirut and Walkmen while keeping Van Etten's raw, plainspoken songwriting at the center. 'Serpents' and 'We Are Fine' widen her folk-based sound with fuller arrangement without smoothing over the emotional bluntness of Epic. It is widely considered her breakthrough record.
Sharon Van Etten.lineage: Expands Epic's confessional folk songwriting with the National's chamber-indie production sensibility, moving Van Etten from lo-fi folk singer toward a fuller indie-rock sound.

Sharp Pins.description: Kai Slater's (Lifeguard, Dwaal Troupe) solo power-pop project delivers bedroom-recorded, Big Star/Teenage Fanclub-style hooks with a scrappy, tape-hiss charm.
Sharp Pins.lineage: Descends from the Big Star power-pop lineage via lo-fi, self-recorded bedroom pop.

Sharp Pins.description: Kai Slater's Sharp Pins project follows Turtle Rock with fourteen driving, Nuggets-indebted power-pop songs, tighter and more melodically direct than before. Calvin Johnson's K Records/Perennial imprint released it, cementing Sharp Pins' place in the Big Star-to-GBV jangle-pop lineage.
Sharp Pins.lineage: Follows Turtle Rock in the 1960s-garage-into-Big-Star jangle-pop lineage, released through Calvin Johnson's K Records/Perennial, tying it directly to that label's power-pop history.

Sharp Pins.description: A sprawling twenty-one-song set from Kai Slater, packed with 1965-styled jangle hooks and endorsed on its sleeve by Robyn Hitchcock. It is the most maximalist Sharp Pins record yet, stringing together short, hook-forward pop songs with barely a pause between them.
Sharp Pins.lineage: Extends Sharp Pins' Nuggets/Big Star-derived jangle-pop into a longer, more song-crammed format, continuing the K Records/Perennial power-pop lineage.

She Returns From War.description: Hunter Park's project She Returns From War bills itself as "Cosmic Americana from South Carolina," and Ruthless leans into dance-pop elements alongside its country roots, cheekily needling Nashville conventions along the way.
She Returns From War.lineage: A Southern songwriter reworking cosmic-country tropes with modern pop production, part of the same Southeastern DIY circuit as Minor Moon and V.V. Lightbody collaborators.

Shearwater.description: Jonathan Meiburg's project, which began as an Okkervil River side band, came fully into its own here with delicate, dynamically extreme songs that swing from near-silence to sudden orchestral swells. It is quieter and more art-song than Okkervil River's records, closer to chamber folk than indie rock.
Shearwater.lineage: Formed out of Okkervil River as a side project for multi-instrumentalist Jonathan Meiburg before becoming its own band with 'Palo Santo'.

Shearwater.description: Shearwater's Matador debut pushed further into orchestral dynamics, with Meiburg's operatic falsetto set against sparse piano and sudden bursts of full-band noise. It is generally considered the peak of the band's Austin-folk-adjacent, pre-art-rock period.
Shearwater.lineage: Continues the dynamically extreme chamber-folk approach of 'Palo Santo' on a larger label with a fuller studio budget.

Sheepskin.description: Pirate Ship Playground is the debut from Burlington duo Molly Meehan and Sam Tiesworth, tasteful dual-vocal folk that recalls the old Canvasback/Asthmatic Kitty era without tipping into twee. Its seven songs favor close harmony and warmth over ornament.
Sheepskin.lineage: Part of the Burlington, Vermont scene around Greg Freeman and vega (Meehan's own solo project), extending that circle's soft-spoken folk-rock.

Shel Silverstein.album: Boy Named Sue (And His Other Country Songs)
Shel Silverstein.description: Best known as a cartoonist and children's author, Shel Silverstein was also a prolific country songwriter, and this album collects his own versions of comic story-songs including 'A Boy Named Sue,' which Johnny Cash turned into a live hit at San Quentin the same year. Produced by Chet Atkins and Felton Jarvis in Nashville, the record leans on the same absurdist, punchline-driven storytelling that made Silverstein's poetry famous, just set to honky-tonk arrangements. It shows how directly the country-storyteller tradition of this lane overlapped with novelty and comedy songwriting.
Shel Silverstein.lineage: Silverstein's Nashville songwriting connections to Johnny Cash and Bobby Bare tie him directly into the outlaw and mainstream country worlds this lane borders, and his comic, plainspoken storytelling is a direct precursor to the funny-sad tradition Prine and Goodman built up at the same time.

Shel Silverstein.description: Freakin' at the Freakers Ball moves Silverstein's comic storytelling from Nashville country parody into early-1970s counterculture satire, skewering drug culture, sex, and hippie pretension with the same singsong bluntness he used in his poetry. 'Sarah Cynthia Sylvia Stout Would Not Take the Garbage Out' later became one of his most famous published poems, showing how directly his song lyrics and children's verse fed each other. Dr. Hook & the Medicine Show, who Silverstein wrote extensively for, later covered the title track, tying this record into the same wry storytelling lineage as Prine and Goodman's Chicago scene.
Shel Silverstein.lineage: Silverstein's dual career as a cartoonist and Nashville country songwriter made him a direct bridge between comic storytelling and country songcraft, an influence later cited by deadpan songwriters in the Prine lineage.

Shep Treasure.description: Blanket is hazy, meditative Rochester folk rock that Josh Terry described as pairing gorgeousness with eeriness and wonkiness, its slow tempos and murky production sitting close to the lane's slowcore-adjacent end.
Shep Treasure.lineage: Follows Shep Treasure's earlier EPs and remix records; vocalist Sabrina Nichols also lends backing vocals to Joyer, tying the two acts to the same East Coast DIY circle.

Shirley Collins and Davy Graham.description: A collaboration between traditional-song singer Shirley Collins and guitar innovator Davy Graham, this album set English and American folk songs like 'Nottamun Town' and 'Reynardine' against Graham's blues- and jazz-inflected fingerstyle guitar, including his own instrumental 'Blue Monk.' Graham's open-tuning, modal approach to the guitar, developed here and on his own records, became foundational for the British fingerstyle players (Jansch, Renbourn, Martyn) who followed him. It predates the main folk-rock era by a few years but is usually cited as the record that made British folk guitar modern.
Shirley Collins and Davy Graham.lineage: A direct root of the British folk-rock and fingerstyle-guitar lineage: Davy Graham's playing here shaped Bert Jansch, John Renbourn and John Martyn, and Collins's song choices fed the repertoire Fairport Convention later electrified.

Shoes.description: Recorded on a four-track in a home studio outside Chicago and self-released on their own label, Shoes built a whole album of Beatles/Big Star-style melodicism out of almost nothing but guitars, tape hiss and three-part harmony. Its lo-fi origins were as influential as its songwriting, a blueprint for DIY pop that predates most of the 1980s home-taping scene by years. It is one of the earliest true bedroom-pop records, hiding genuinely gorgeous hooks under deliberately modest means.
Shoes.lineage: An early, largely self-made extension of the Big Star/Beatles jangle-pop sound, notable for pairing that melodic lineage with a DIY home-recording ethic that anticipated the 1980s-90s lo-fi underground.

Shoes.description: Signed to a major label after Black Vinyl Shoes built a cult following, Shoes cleaned up their sound without losing the plain, close-harmony charm that made the debut work, landing squarely in the classic late-1970s power-pop mold. "Tomorrow Night" (re-recorded from the debut) and "Too Late" show a band comfortable writing hooks that sound both effortless and slightly melancholy. It remains one of the era's most purely melodic records, a quieter cousin to Cheap Trick's louder version of the same instincts.
Shoes.lineage: Represents the studio-polished, major-label counterpart to Shoes' own DIY debut, part of the same late-1970s power-pop wave as the Records and 20/20.

Shoulderbird.description: Neighbors is Meredith Nesbitt's second Shoulderbird album, eight modest, intimate tracks of folksy Midwest Americana written and recorded at home about moving, displacement and holding onto family. It favors plainspoken detail over ornament.
Shoulderbird.lineage: Nesbitt also plays in Hannah Frances' and Minor Moon's bands, tying Shoulderbird to Chicago's hushed folk-rock network.

Shrunken Elvis.description: An instrumental trio of Nashville sidemen (Spencer Cullum on pedal steel, Sean Thompson on guitar, Rich Ruth's Michael Ruth on synths) built this debut from a European tour's worth of long-drive jamming. It luxuriates in kosmische, ambient and jazz-fusion textures rather than song structure -- Dead-adjacent in spirit, closer to Alice Coltrane or Ashra in execution.
Shrunken Elvis.lineage: Formed from the overlapping session circles of Nashville's Promised Land Sound/Erin Rae/Margo Price world; a spinoff project of Spencer Cullum's Coin Collection and Sean Thompson's Weird Ears.

Sierra Ferrell.description: A West Virginia-to-Nashville songwriter whose sound blends bluegrass and old-time instrumentation with vintage country, gypsy-jazz, and folk textures, Trail of Flowers swept the 2024 Americana Music Awards. Her flexible, old-timey-inflected voice moves between wistful balladry and rowdy string-band numbers without settling into one lane. It is for hearing bluegrass and old-time tradition filtered through a genuinely idiosyncratic, festival-scale voice.
Sierra Ferrell.lineage: A genre-blurring newgrass/old-time descendant that shares Molly Tuttle's and Billy Strings's current bluegrass-revival moment while pulling in vintage pop and gypsy-jazz textures closer to X2's arena-Americana crossover audience.

Silkworm.description: Silkworm's Matador debut pairs Tim Midyett and Andy Cohen's dual songwriting and dry, conversational baritones with lean, muscular guitar interplay, closer to a smarter, more literate Superchunk than to their noise-rock peers. The songs are direct and unshowy, built around riffs rather than hooks, with lyrics that read like short stories. It marked the band's arrival on the national indie stage after years as a Pacific Northwest cult act.
Silkworm.lineage: Formed from the band's Missoula-to-Seattle relocation, Firewater is Silkworm's step up to Matador Records alongside labelmates Pavement and Yo La Tengo, cementing their move from regional to national indie profile.

Silkworm.description: Developer keeps Silkworm's twin-vocalist, riff-driven approach intact while tightening the songwriting further, with Andy Cohen and Tim Midyett's contrasting voices trading off across terse, unsentimental rock songs. It is a transitional record between the band's Matador years and their subsequent move to Touch and Go, still carrying the dry Montana-bred wit that ran through all their work. Critics of the era praised its economy and lack of indulgence.
Silkworm.lineage: The last Silkworm album on Matador before the band's move to Touch and Go Records for Blueblood, continuing the lean, literate guitar-rock style the band built out of Missoula and Seattle's underground scenes.

Silkworm.description: Silkworm's Touch and Go debut, made after the band relocated to Chicago, sharpens their riff-first approach with producer Steve Albini's characteristically dry, live-sounding engineering. Tim Midyett and Andy Cohen's songwriting stays plainspoken and unsentimental, closer to a bar-band version of Silver Jews than to anything flashy. It is often cited by fans as the point where the band's Chicago-era identity solidified.
Silkworm.lineage: Marks Silkworm's move from Matador to Touch and Go Records and from Seattle to Chicago, aligning the band with the Albini-adjacent Midwest noise-rock and indie-rock underground of the late 1990s.

Silkworm.description: Lifestyle sharpens Silkworm's Chicago-era sound into some of the band's most direct and emotionally clear-eyed songwriting, with Midyett and Cohen's dry vocal delivery carrying lyrics about domestic disappointment and adult compromise. The guitar interplay stays lean and riff-driven, avoiding any of the era's more fashionable noise-rock excess. It is frequently cited by longtime fans as a high point of the band's Touch and Go run.
Silkworm.lineage: Continues Silkworm's Touch and Go, Albini-adjacent Chicago period, extending the band's 1990s Matador-era sound into the new decade without significant change in approach.

Silkworm.description: Italian Platinum keeps Silkworm's dual-vocalist songwriting formula while opening up slightly more melodic space on tracks like 'Young Cannons.' It is a confident, road-tested record from a band deep into its second decade together, still built on riffs and plainspoken storytelling rather than studio polish. The album continued the critical respect the band had built without ever translating into wider commercial recognition.
Silkworm.lineage: A later, confident entry in Silkworm's Touch and Go catalog, carrying the Missoula-bred band's lean guitar-rock sound into the early 2000s alongside labelmates like Braid and the Jesus Lizard.

Silkworm.description: Silkworm's third album is the last to feature Joel R.L. Phelps alongside Tim Midyett and Andy Cohen, and it carries more of his rawer, more anguished delivery than the band's later Matador records. The guitar interplay is still lean and riff-driven, but the mood is darker and more turbulent, closer to the band's noise-rock roots. 'Couldn't You Wait?' and 'Cotton Girl' show the push-pull between the band's three songwriting voices.
Silkworm.lineage: Recorded during Silkworm's Missoula-to-Seattle years just before Phelps' departure, Libertine is the transitional record between the band's rougher early sound and the more streamlined Matador albums that followed.

Silver Jews.description: David Berman's first full-length as Silver Jews, cut with Pavement's Stephen Malkmus and Bob Nastanovich on guitar and drums, is a loose, hissy, half-shambling record where Berman's flat, talk-sung baritone reads like poetry set to a barely-rehearsed bar band. Verses wander into non-sequiturs and one-liners before landing on something genuinely aching, a formula that became the band's signature. It is for listeners who want indie rock's slack, in-joke energy turned toward plainspoken, literary songwriting.
Silver Jews.lineage: Grows out of the Pavement/Drag City slacker-rock axis (Malkmus and Nastanovich as sidemen) crossed with Prine- and Dylan-style talking-blues songwriting; it set the template Berman would refine through American Water and that later Drag City deadpan artists like Bill Callahan and Will Oldham worked alongside.

Silver Jews.description: Recorded without Malkmus, this second Silver Jews album strips the band down to a shakier, sadder core, with Berman's voice sitting low in the mix over simple, unhurried guitar figures. Stephen Malkmus once singled out 'Pretty Eyes' as one of the best songs of its decade, and the record's mix of dry humor and real desolation set the emotional register Berman would return to for the rest of his career. A key record for anyone tracing how slacker-rock detachment curdled into genuine heartbreak.
Silver Jews.lineage: Follows directly from Starlite Walker but trades Pavement's band chemistry for a barer, more personal sound, pointing toward the full-band country-rock of American Water and influencing later Drag City songwriters who prized plainspoken sadness over polish.

Silver Jews.description: Widely considered the Silver Jews' masterpiece, this reunites Berman with Malkmus on guitar for a fuller, more confident sound while keeping the deadpan delivery and aphoristic lyrics that made the band's reputation. 'Random Rules' opens with one of indie rock's most quoted first lines, and the record balances slacker guitar interplay with genuine tenderness and dread. It is the field guide's suggested entry point into the whole Drag City deadpan school.
